definitions.text: To deprive of hair, or of hairs; as, to unhair hides for leather. I 'll unhair thy head. Shak.
To profane; to desecrate. The vanity unhallows the virtue. L'Estrange.
Not consecrated; hence, profane; unholy; impious; wicked. In the cause of truth, no unhallowed violence . . . is either necessary or admissible. E. D. Griffin.
To loose from the hand; to let go. Hold off! unhand me, gray beard loon! Eftsoons his hand dropped he. Coleridge.

Not handsome; not beautiful; ungraceful; not comely or pleasing; plain; homely. Were she other than she is, she were unhandsome. Shak. I can not admit that there is anything unhandsome or irregular . . . in the globe. Woodward.
Wanting noble or amiable qualities; dishonorable; illiberal; low; disingenuous; mean; indecorous; as, unhandsome conduct, treatment, or imputations. "Unhandsome pleasures." J. Fletcher.

Unhandy; clumsy; awkward; inconvenient. [Obs.] The ships were unwieldy and unhandsome. Holland. A narrow, straight path by the water's side, very unhandsome for an army to pass that way, though they found not a man to keep the
Clumsy; awkward; as, an Unhandy man.
To divest or strip of hangings; to remove the hangings, as a room.
To remove (something hanging or swinging) from that which supports it; as, to unhang a gate.
Ill luck; misfortune. [Obs.] "The cause of her unhap." Sir P. Sidney.
Made unhappy. [Obs.] Shak.
Not happy or fortunate; unfortunate; unlucky; as, affairs have taken an unhappy turn.
In a degree miserable or wretched; not happy; sad; sorrowful; as, children render their parents unhappy by misconduct.
Marked by infelicity; evil; calamitous; as, an unhappy day. "The unhappy morn." Milton.
Mischievous; wanton; wicked. [Obs.] Shak.
To drive from harbor or shelter.
Having no harbor or shelter; unprotected.
Affording no harbor or shelter. "Unharbored heaths." [Obs.] Milton.
Inharmonious; unsymmetrical; also, unmusical; discordant.
To strip of harness; to loose from harness or gear; as, to unharness horses or oxen. Cowper.
To disarm; to divest of armor. Holinshed.
To unloose the hasp of; to unclose.
To take off the hat of; to remove one's hat, especially as a mark of respect. H. Spenser.
To take out the head of; as, to unhead a cask.
To decapitate; to behead. [Obs.] T. Brown.
Misfortune; calamity; sickness. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To uncover. See Unhele. [Obs.]
Unsoundness; disease.
Not heard; not perceived by the ear; as, words unheard by those present.

Not granted an audience or a hearing; not allowed to speak; not having made a defense, or stated one's side of a question; disregarded; unheeded; as, to condemunheard. What pangs I feel, unpitied and unheard! Dryden.

Not known to fame; not illustrious or celebrated; obscure. Nor was his name unheard or unadored. Milton. Unheard of. (a) Not heard of; of which there are no tidings. (b) Unknown to fame; obscure. Glanvill.
New; unprecedented; unparalleled. Swift.
To cause to lose heart; to dishearten. [Obs.] Shak.
Incautious; precipitate; heedless. [Obs.] Milton.
Destitute of an heir. To leave him utterly unheired. Chapman.
Same as Unheal, n. [Obs.]
To uncover. [Obs.] Spenser. Marston.
To deprive of the helm or helmet. Sir W. Scott.
Etym: [Properly p. p. of unhelm.]
Divested or deprived of the helm or helmet.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + helm.]
Not wearing a helmet; without a helmet. Sir W. Scott.
To deprive of the helmet. Sir W. Scott.
To bring out from concealment; to discover. [Obs.] P. Fletcher.
To take from the hinges; as, to unhinge a door.
To displace; to unfix by violence. Blackmore.

To render unstable or wavering; to unsettle; as, to unhinge one's mind or opinions; to unhinge the nerves. Why should I then unhinge my brains, ruin my mind South. His sufferings, nay the revolutions of his fate, had not in the least unhinged his mind. Walpole.
The act unhinging, or the state of being unhinged.
To free from being hitched, or as if from being hitched; to unfasten; to loose; as, to unhitch a horse, or a trace.
To drive or remove from a hive.
To deprive of habitation or shelter, as a crowd.
To take or steal from a hoard; to pilfer. Milton.
To cease to hold; to unhand; to release. [Obs.] Otway.
Not holy; unhallowed; not consecrated; hence, profane; wicked;
To remove a hood or disguise from. Quarterly Rev.
To loose from a hook; to undo or open by loosening or unfastening the hooks of; as, to unhook a fish; to unhook a dress.
To strip or deprive of hoops; to take away the hoops of.
Not hoped or expected. "With unhoped success." Dryden. Blessings of friends, which to my door Unasked, unhoped, have come. J. N. Newman.
Unhoped; unexpected.
To throw from a horse; to cause to dismount; also, to take a horse or horses from; as, to unhorse a rider; to unhorse a carriage. Cowper.
Without hose.
Inhospitable.
To drive from a house or habitation; to dislodge; hence, to deprive of shelter.
Etym: [Properly p. p. of unhouse.]
Driven from a house; deprived of shelter.
Etym: [Pref. un- + housed.]
Not provided with a house or shelter; houseless; homeless.
Not having received the sacrament. [Obs.] [Written also unhouselled.] To die like the houseless dog on yonder common, unshriven and unhouseled. Sir W. Scott.
Not human; inhuman.
To render inhuman or barbarous. J. Barlow.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + husked.]
